entries_new.name: Sentinelese of North Sentinel Island
entries_new.pop: Estimates of 50 to 200, wider estimates up to 500
entries_new.challenge: India claims the island but has stopped visits and bans approach
entries_new.mechanism: They reject outsiders, and Indian law now seals the island off rather than administering it.
entries_new.story:
The Sentinelese are an Indigenous people on North Sentinel Island in the Andaman Islands, which India governs in the Bay of Bengal. They never asked for statehood, and India counts the island as its own. In practice no official has ruled there. A 1956 regulation made the island a tribal reserve and bans travel within 5 km, and India keeps an armed patrol in the surrounding waters. Indian visits stopped in 1997.
Census counts have ranged from 15 to 117, and wider estimates reach 500. An American missionary was killed in 2018 while visiting illegally. A US citizen who landed without permission was arrested in 2025. Survival International warns that outside diseases could wipe out the people.
entries_new.anchor: Andaman Islands, Bay of Bengal (region only)

entries_new.name: Nomole people of Madre de Dios
entries_new.challenge: Logging concessions and oil and gas exploration
entries_new.mechanism: They retreated from rubber-era violence into forest that the state does not administer day to day.
entries_new.story: The Nomole are nomadic hunter-gatherers in the Madre de Dios region of the Peruvian Amazon, also known by a name they consider derogatory, Mashco Piro. In the rubber boom of the 1890s the private army of the rubber baron Carlos Fitzcarrald slaughtered many of them, and the survivors withdrew into remote forest. Estimates rose from 100 to 250 in 1998 to above 750 in 2024. Peru has banned contact with them because of the disease risk. In July 2024 Survival International published images of them a few kilometres from logging concessions, and in September 2024 at least two loggers were killed by an uncontacted Nomole group.
entries_new.anchor: Madre de Dios region, Peru (region only)

entries_new.name: Isolated peoples of the Vale do Javari
entries_new.recognition: Brazil protects the territory under its own law
entries_new.mechanism: Brazil seals the territory in its own law and leaves the peoples inside uncontacted.
entries_new.story: The Vale do Javari is an Indigenous territory of 85,444 square km in western Amazonas, Brazil. In the 1960s and 1970s Brazil tried to assimilate Amazon peoples so their land could be farmed. It changed course in 1987, creating a Department of Isolated Indians inside FUNAI, its Indigenous affairs agency, and declaring the Vale do Javari perpetually sealed off. The Korubu, the Flecheiros and the Tsohom Djapa live there without contact. FUNAI reported receiving only 15% of its requested budget in 2017.

entries_new.name: Kawahiva of the Rio Pardo
entries_new.challenge: Their land rights depended on a Brazilian court order for demarcation
entries_new.mechanism: They keep moving and avoid outsiders, while advocates use Brazilian courts to get the land marked out.
entries_new.story: The Kawahiva are a small people in the north of Mato Grosso, Brazil, known mostly from what they leave behind: arrows, baskets, hammocks and communal houses. Their population was estimated at 15 in 2016 and 35 to 40 in 2024. The government released video of them filmed in 2011. After years of campaigning, Brazil's Supreme Court in 2024 ordered FUNAI, the Indigenous affairs agency, to give a timetable for marking out the Kawahiva do Rio Pardo territory, and in March 2025 FUNAI said it meant to finish by the end of 2025.

entries_new.name: Awá of Maranhão
entries_new.mechanism: Part of the people stays out of contact in the forest inside a state that claims the land.
entries_new.story: The Awá live in Maranhão in north-east Brazil. There are about 350 of them, of whom roughly 100 have no contact with the outside world. Violent conflict with loggers in their territory puts them at severe risk. In 1982 the Brazilian government received a US$900 million loan from the World Bank and the European Union on condition that the lands of certain Indigenous peoples, including the Awá, would be marked out and protected. It took 20 years of pressure from campaign groups before the Awá's land was marked out in March 2003.

entries_new.name: Man of the Hole, Tanaru territory
entries_new.mechanism: He lived alone on land held as a Brazilian Indigenous territory.
entries_new.story: The man known as the Man of the Hole lived alone on 8,000 hectares in the Tanaru Indigenous Territory in Rondônia, Brazil. He dug hundreds of holes for farming and trapping, which gave him the name. He was found dead in his hammock, in a dwelling he built, in August 2022. The land remained a Brazilian Indigenous territory throughout.

entries_new.name: Piripkura survivors
entries_new.mechanism: Two brothers stayed in the forest out of contact until they chose to approach the agency.
entries_new.story: The Piripkura are a people in Mato Grosso, Brazil, of whom three members are recorded as surviving. Two brothers kept living alone in the forest, and they approached FUNAI, the Indigenous affairs agency, after a fire they had kept burning for 18 years went out. Their case was the subject of the documentary Piripkura.

entries_new.name: Panará and the BR-163 road
entries_new.mechanism: Distance kept them apart until a government road crossed their land.
entries_new.story: The Panará are a people of the Brazilian Amazon who lived in relative isolation until 1973, when the government built the Cuiabá to Santarém road, BR-163, through their territory. Of more than 350 Panará, more than 250 died in the first twelve months after first contact with settlers, from newly introduced diseases. Land damage followed.

entries_new.name: Toromona of Madidi
entries_new.challenge: Mining encroachment reported in Bolivia in 2016
entries_new.recognition: Bolivia reserves part of a national park for them under its own law
entries_new.mechanism: A national park zone is closed to others in Bolivian law.
entries_new.story: The Toromona are an uncontacted people near the upper Madidi and Heath rivers in north-west Bolivia. Bolivia has created an "exclusive, reserved, and inviolable" portion of Madidi National Park to protect them. Bolivia has 13 groups of isolated peoples, of which three live on land with legal protection recognised by the government. A Chinese subsidiary mining company in Bolivia was reported in 2016 to have ignored signs that it was encroaching on uncontacted groups.

entries_new.name: Nukak of the Guaviare
entries_new.stopped_by: Disease, armed conflict and forced relocation by Colombia
entries_new.mechanism: They kept to the forest until a missionary group made contact.
entries_new.story: The Nukak are nomadic hunter-gatherers between the Guaviare and Inírida rivers in south-east Colombia. An evangelical group made contact with them, and they moved closer to settlers to trade. Respiratory infections followed, along with violent clashes with drug traffickers, and hundreds died, more than half of the people. The Colombian government then forcibly moved them to a nearby town, where they received food and state support and were reported to be living in poverty.

entries_new.name: Tagaeri and Taromenane of Yasuní
entries_new.mechanism: Ecuadorian policy sets a rule of no contact around peoples who avoid it anyway.
entries_new.story: The Tagaeri and Taromenane are two isolated peoples in Yasuní National Park in the Ecuadorian Amazon, both eastern Huaorani. They are semi-nomadic and live in small groups of extended families. Since 2007 Ecuador has had a national policy requiring untouchability, self-determination, equality and no contact. In 2013 more than 20 Taromenane were killed by Waorani, another Huaorani group.

entries_new.name: Ayoreo Totobiegosode of the Chaco
entries_new.challenge: Deforestation and ranch conversion of their land
entries_new.mechanism: Small nomadic groups avoid outsiders while contacted relatives argue their case before an international body.
entries_new.story: About 100 Ayoreo people, some of them Totobiegosode, live uncontacted in the Paraguayan Chaco. They are the last uncontacted peoples south of the Amazon basin. According to Survival International, the Brazilian company Yaguarete Porá S.A. is converting thousands of hectares of their ancestral land to cattle ranching. Other Ayoreo, through the Union of Ayoreo Natives of Paraguay, work for their protection, and in 2021 the Ayoreo appealed to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. A YouTuber's repeated attempts to reach them were reported by Survival.

entries_new.name: O'Hongana Manyawa of Halmahera
entries_new.mechanism: They stay in the island interior and tell companies directly to keep out.
entries_new.story: The O'Hongana Manyawa, also called Inner Tobelo or Togutil, are a semi-nomadic people in the interior of Halmahera Island in North Maluku, Indonesia. In October 2023 footage emerged of members warning logging companies to stay away from their land. A 2024 report claimed their forest was being destroyed by the nickel mining industry.

entries_new.name: Shompen of Great Nicobar
entries_new.mechanism: They stay in the forested interior of an island that India administers from the coast.
entries_new.story: The Shompen live in the interior of Great Nicobar Island, in India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands. In 2001 they numbered about 300. Survival International calls them among the most isolated peoples on earth. India's Great Nicobar Development Plan proposes an airport, an international port and an industrial park on the island. In February 2024, 39 genocide experts from 13 countries warned that it "will be a death sentence for the Shompen", because the people have little or no immunity to outside diseases. The plan is being contested in court.

entries_new.name: Inner Baduy of Kanekes
entries_new.mechanism: Internal rules sort the people into rings with different levels of outside contact.
entries_new.story: The Baduy, or Kanekes, live in Banten on the Indonesian island of Java. They divide into Tangtu (Inner Baduy), Panamping (Outer Baduy) and Dangka. The Inner Baduy shun all contact with outsiders, and the Outer Baduy keep limited contact. The Dangka live outside the Kanekes area and have regular contact with the outside world.

entries_new.name: Zomia
entries_new.founder: Term coined by Willem van Schendel
entries_new.pop: About 100 million in the wider massif
entries_new.mechanism: People moved uphill, beyond the reach of lowland tax collectors and armies, according to Scott's argument.
entries_new.story: Zomia is a name coined in 2002 by the historian Willem van Schendel for the highlands of mainland Southeast Asia that lowland governments have historically not controlled. It takes in north Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, the Shan Hills of Myanmar and south-west China, and some scholars extend it further. James C. Scott argued in his 2009 book The Art of Not Being Governed that hill peoples are "runaway, fugitive, maroon communities" who fled slavery, conscription, taxes and forced labour over two millennia, and that this era is ending. Jean Michaud and others use the neutral term Southeast Asian Massif, home to about 100 million Indigenous people and never united politically.

entries_new.name: Somalia without a central state, 1991 to 2006
entries_new.stopped_by: Transitional governments from 2000 and 2004, and the Ethiopian invasion of 2006
entries_new.mechanism: No group replaced the state, so clans, courts and regional governments filled the gap.
entries_new.story: Clan-based armed groups overthrew Somalia's government under Siad Barre in 1991, and no central government replaced it. In 1990 to 1992 customary law also broke down and factions fought across the south. UN missions arrived in 1992 and withdrew in 1995. After that, customary and religious law returned in most regions. Somaliland (1991) and Puntland (1998) set up their own governments in the north, and Sharia courts spread in the south. SIPRI, a Swedish peace research institute, took Somalia off its list of major armed conflicts for 1997 and 1998. Transitional governments formed in 2000 and 2004, and Ethiopian troops invaded in 2006.

entries_new.name: Xeer, Somali customary law
entries_new.mechanism: Clan groups settle disputes through elders and compensation payments, with no state court required.
entries_new.story: Xeer is the traditional legal system used by Somalis in Djibouti, Somalia, Somaliland, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and north-eastern Kenya. Elders act as mediator judges and rely on precedent and custom, and different groups interpret it differently. Crimes count as wrongs against property, and the remedy is material compensation to the victim. Each member of a mag group, a small unit of kin or contract, helps pay if the accused cannot. Only the victim or close family may bring a case, and a woman's complaint must come through men in her family or her husband's.
entries_new.anchor: Somali-speaking regions of the Horn of Africa

entries_new.name: Islamic Courts Union
entries_new.challenge: A CIA-backed warlord alliance, then Ethiopia
entries_new.mechanism: Neighbourhood courts pooled their militias and money, then took over from the warlords.
entries_new.story: The Islamic Courts Union was an alliance of Sharia courts in Mogadishu, Somalia. After the state collapsed in 1991, neighbourhood courts formed to impose order, and warlord threats pushed them to unite by 2000. Somali businesses funded them. In summer 2006 the alliance defeated a warlord coalition backed by the CIA, becoming the first group to hold all of Mogadishu since the collapse, and it then acted as the government of most of southern and central Somalia. In December 2006, after UN Security Council Resolution 1725, Ethiopian troops invaded to install the Transitional Federal Government, and the union disintegrated.

entries_new.name: Cantons of the Lebanese Civil War
entries_new.stopped_by: Taif Agreement, 1989, and the disbanding of most militias after 1990
entries_new.mechanism: Militias ran services, prices and policing on the land they held while no government could stop them.
entries_new.story: As central government in Lebanon fell apart in the civil war, parties and militias set up full administrations on the land they held. These were called cantons, after the self-governing Swiss provinces. The best known was "Marounistan", held by the Phalangists and Lebanese Forces around East Beirut. The Marada area around Zghorta was the "Northern Canton". A TIME correspondent who visited East Beirut in 1976 reported clean streets and petrol at one fifth of the West Beirut price. The 1989 Taif Agreement led to most militias being disbanded by 1990. Hezbollah kept its weapons, citing resistance to Israel's occupation in the south.

entries_new.name: Civil Administration of the Mountain
entries_new.stopped_by: Taif Agreement and end of the civil war
entries_new.mechanism: An armed party governed its home district while the state was absent.
entries_new.story: The Civil Administration of the Mountain was a Druze-dominated territory in Lebanon led by Walid Jumblatt, from 1983 until it wore away after the Taif Agreement and the end of the civil war. The People's Liberation Army, armed wing of Jumblatt's Progressive Socialist Party, held most of the Chouf district and parts of Aley and Baabda. It bordered the East Beirut canton held by the rival Lebanese Forces. It ran a radio station, the Voice of the Mountain, from 1984 to 1994.

entries_new.name: State of Free Lebanon
entries_new.mechanism: A local commander declared a state on the border and relied on a neighbouring country for support.
entries_new.story: Free Lebanon was an unrecognised state in southern Lebanon, proclaimed on 18 April 1979 by the Lebanese officer Saad Haddad during the civil war. The Lebanese government called him a traitor and dismissed him from the army the next day. It depended on Israeli logistics and, after 1982, military support, and Wikipedia's account calls it a puppet state of Israel. Its authority declined after Haddad died in 1984. A Christian administration and the South Lebanon Army carried on under Israeli supervision inside the 1985 to 2000 occupation zone and collapsed when Israel withdrew in 2000.

entries_new.name: Libya's rival governments, 2014 to 2020
entries_new.recognition: The international community recognised the Tobruk government first and the Government of National Accord after 2015
entries_new.mechanism: Rival parliaments each claimed to be the whole state and held the zones their armed allies controlled.
entries_new.story: After a disputed 2014 election Libya had two parliaments. The new General National Congress held Tripoli and Misrata in the west, and the House of Representatives sat in Tobruk in the east, backed by General Khalifa Haftar's forces. Foreign states backed both sides: Qatar and Turkey the first, Egypt and the UAE the second. A December 2015 agreement at Skhirat created the UN-backed Government of National Accord, but armed groups continued fighting, among them the Islamic State's Libyan branches. A permanent ceasefire came on 23 October 2020 and an interim unity government on 10 March 2021.

entries_new.name: Greater Liberia
entries_new.challenge: Rival militias, and the Interim Government of National Unity
entries_new.mechanism: A rebel commander built a state's departments on captured land and financed it from exports.
entries_new.story: Greater Liberia, or Taylorland, was the area held by Charles Taylor's National Patriotic Front during Liberia's first civil war, as the central government collapsed. The group took its first town, Butuo, on 24 December 1989 and made Gbarnga its capital. At its peak it held 90% of the country. Taylor set up a civilian government, the NPRAG, and a justice system under his control. The area had its own currency, banks, broadcasters, airfields and, until 1993, a deepwater port, with exports of diamonds, timber and gold. Taylor won the war and was elected President of Liberia, so his rebel area became the state.

entries_new.name: Syrian Salvation Government
entries_new.mechanism: An armed group ran a civilian administration in one corner of a collapsing state, then took the capital.
entries_new.story: The Syrian Salvation Government was an unrecognised administration in north-west Syria, formed on 2 November 2017 by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), an armed group, and other opposition groups during the civil war. Its capital in practice was Idlib, and it had a population estimated at over 4 million in 2023, with a Shura Council and a prime minister. Before it, a patchwork of armed groups and local councils ran the governorate. After Damascus fell in December 2024, the last Ba'athist prime minister handed power to its prime minister, and its ministers took the same posts in the caretaker government of Syria.

entries_new.name: Viv Ansanm in Port-au-Prince
entries_new.mechanism: Rival gangs merged and pushed the state out of most of a capital city.
entries_new.story: Viv Ansanm is a coalition of armed gangs in Haiti, created by the former police officer Jimmy Chérizier, known as Barbecue. A first alliance in September 2023 fell apart within weeks, and on 29 February 2024 the G9 and G-Pèp umbrella groups united. It controls about 80% of metropolitan Port-au-Prince and many nearby towns, and it attacks police stations and government buildings. It was formed partly to resist foreign security forces authorised by the UN Security Council. Chérizier describes it as opposing the Haitian and American oligarchs and demanding dialogue with the government.

entries_new.name: Prince Wilhelm of Wied, chosen for Albania
entries_new.stopped_by: Loss of foreign funding and departure in September 1914
entries_new.recognition: The Great Powers that selected him
entries_new.mechanism: Foreign powers picked a ruler for a new country, and he depended on their money.
entries_new.story: When Albania broke from the Ottoman Empire in 1912, six Great Powers, among them Britain, France and Germany, looked for an aristocrat to rule it. The queen of Romania lobbied for her nephew, Wilhelm of Wied, a Prussian officer. He turned the offer down in spring 1913, then accepted under Austrian pressure, and the choice was announced that November. He reigned from 7 March to 3 September 1914. His pay was cut off when he refused to send Albanian soldiers into the First World War, citing the country's neutrality under the Treaty of London. He left saying he was absent "temporarily", and his title ended officially when Albania became a republic in 1925.

entries_new.name: Otto Witte's claim to the Albanian throne
entries_new.mechanism: A self-told impersonation story, later given a small official echo on an identity card.
entries_new.story: Otto Witte was a German circus acrobat who said he had been crowned King of Albania by local troops on 13 August 1913, by posing as a nephew of the Ottoman Sultan named Halim Eddine. He said he reigned five days, kept a harem, declared war on Montenegro and escaped with part of the treasury. Most of this was found to be impossible: there was no Halim Eddine, he changed the date once, and no local evidence supports him. The Berlin police still let his identity card carry the words "former King of Albania", and the title is on his tombstone in Hamburg.

entries_new.name: House of Grimaldi in Monaco
entries_new.mechanism: A family seized a fortress, then traded land and foreign-policy freedom for lasting recognition.
entries_new.story: The Grimaldis, an ousted Genoese family, captured the rock of Monaco in 1297 by posing as monks, then fought for a century for official control. Genoa, France and Spain later let the family keep it under agreements, largely on defence. France annexed it during the Revolution. In 1861 Monaco sold Menton and Roquebrune, about 95% of its land, to France for 4,100,000 francs, and France recognised its sovereignty. Under a July 1918 treaty, which also settled a succession crisis, Monaco's international policy was aligned with French interests. A 2002 treaty says Monaco stays independent if the dynasty has no heirs. It has been a full UN member since 1993.

entries_new.name: Duke of Mecklenburg and the United Baltic Duchy
entries_new.mechanism: An occupying army's local allies offered a throne to a prince from the occupier's own nobility.
entries_new.story: The United Baltic Duchy was a German client state proclaimed in Riga on 5 November 1918 by Baltic German leaders, on land under German military occupation in Courland, Livonia and Estonia. Its throne was offered to Duke Adolf Friedrich of Mecklenburg, an explorer of Africa and last governor of German Togoland. He stayed in Germany and never took it. Germany lost the war within days, Estonia and Latvia emerged in the region, and the regency council was abolished on 28 November 1918.

entries_new.name: Wilhelm of Urach, elected King Mindaugas II of Lithuania
entries_new.stopped_by: German refusal to recognise the election
entries_new.mechanism: A national council elected a foreign prince to win independence from the occupying empire.
entries_new.story: On 4 June 1918 the Council of Lithuania voted to invite Wilhelm, Duke of Urach, a German general, to be king of a newly independent Lithuania. He accepted and was elected on 11 July as Mindaugas II. He was a Roman Catholic, as most Lithuanians were, and not a Hohenzollern, the German emperor's family. He agreed to live in Lithuania and learn the language. Four socialists on the 20-member council quit in protest. The German government declared the election invalid, the invitation was withdrawn in November 1918, and he never took the crown.

entries_new.name: Frederick Charles of Hesse, elected King of Finland
entries_new.mechanism: An elected monarchy offered to a relative of the German emperor.
entries_new.story: Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse, brother-in-law of the German Emperor Wilhelm II, was elected King of Finland on 9 October 1918. He renounced the throne on 14 December 1918, about two months later. His son Wolfgang was the designated crown prince until the same date.

entries_new.name: Otto of Bavaria, King of Greece
entries_new.mechanism: Foreign guarantors installed a teenage foreign prince on a new throne.
entries_new.story: Otto, second son of King Ludwig of Bavaria, became King of Greece aged 17 when the kingdom was set up on 7 May 1832 under the Convention of London. A regency of three Bavarian officials ran the government at first. He removed them when they proved unpopular and ruled as an absolute monarch until an armed but bloodless uprising forced a constitution on him in 1843. Greek politics of the time ran on loyalty to the three Great Powers that guaranteed the country's independence, Britain, France and Russia. He was deposed in October 1862.
